root_cause.text: In the 802.1q VLAN egress priority mapping code (`vlan_dev_set_egress_priority()`), clearing a mapping did not remove the `vlan_priority_tci_mapping` node from `vlan->egress_priority_map`, so repeated set/clear operations left dead “tombstone” entries behind and caused unbounded memory growth until device teardown.
root_cause.evidence: The commit message says the function “currently keeps cleared egress priority mappings in the hash as tombstones” and that “Repeated set/clear cycles with distinct skb priorities therefore accumulate mapping nodes until device teardown and leak memory”; the patch changes the clear case from just zeroing `mp->vlan_qos` to unlinking the node with `rcu_assign_pointer(*mpp, rtnl_dereference(mp->next));`, decrementing `nr_egress_mappings`, and freeing it via `kfree_rcu(mp, rcu)`, and it also stops creating a new node when `vlan_qos` is cleared (`if (!vlan_qos) return 0;`).

intent_record.intent_summary: Fix egress VLAN priority mapping updates so zero QoS removes entries instead of leaving invalid mappings behind.
intent_record.what: The function now keeps a pointer-to-pointer to the current egress priority map entry, updates list links through that pointer, and when an existing mapping is found with a zero VLAN QoS value it removes that mapping from the bucket, decrements the mapping count, and frees it with kfree_rcu(). It also stops incrementing the mapping count on updates, and returns early without allocating a new mapping when vlan_qos is zero.
intent_record.how: At runtime, setting an egress priority mapping to zero now deletes the existing mapping instead of storing a zero-valued entry, which prevents stale no-op mappings from remaining in the table. Nonzero mappings still get updated in place, and new entries are only created for nonzero VLAN priorities, keeping the map and nr_egress_mappings consistent.

intent_record.intent_summary: Include zero-valued VLAN QoS mappings in netlink VLAN जानकारी instead of skipping them.
intent_record.what: The diff removes an `if (!vlan_qos) continue;` check from the `vlan_fill_info()` loop that iterates over `vlan->egress_priority_map[i]`, so entries with `vlan_qos == 0` are no longer skipped before being added to the netlink message.
intent_record.how: At runtime, VLAN QoS mapping entries whose stored QoS value is zero will now be included in the exported VLAN information instead of being silently omitted. This changes the reported netlink state by making zero-valued mappings visible to userspace.

relevance_review.reason: The change directly matches the root cause: it fixes egress VLAN priority mapping updates so clearing a QoS mapping removes the entry instead of leaving dead tombstones in the egress priority map, preventing the memory growth issue.

The change only affects netlink reporting of VLAN QoS mappings by including zero-valued entries. It does not modify the egress priority mapping set/clear path or address the failure to remove stale nodes from vlan->egress_priority_map that caused the memory leak.

candidates.rationale: This updates an existing mapping in place even when vlan_qos becomes zero, but does not remove the mapping node from egress_priority_map. As a result, clearing a mapping leaves a dead entry behind, causing tombstone accumulation and memory growth.

This conditional detects the clear-to-zero case, but the pre-fix handling only decremented the counter and still kept the node linked in the map. The missing removal is the root cause of lingering tombstone entries.

Only the count was updated on clear, while the actual mapping object remained in the bucket list. This reflects the flawed behavior that allowed repeated set/clear cycles to retain dead mapping nodes.

vuln_statements.explanation: This is the clear-to-zero path for an existing egress priority mapping. In the vulnerable code, it only adjusted accounting instead of removing the mapping node, which left tombstone entries in vlan->egress_priority_map and caused unbounded memory growth.
This line shows the pre-fix clear handling only decremented the mapping count. Because the node itself was not deleted from the map, repeated set/clear operations accumulated dead mapping entries.

This updates the existing mapping in place even when vlan_qos becomes zero. The root cause is that clearing a mapping should remove the node, but this statement leaves the mapping object linked, contributing to tombstone accumulation.
